name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 48

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

blocks.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
one's standing or status in a hierarchy

explanation.surface: An oddball Tory politician who refuses to sit down.
explanation.definitionFit: A crank is a person with odd, obsessive ideas, so the noun is a synonym for an eccentric.

clue.text: After raising hat, single man's attentive

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something lifts it so its letters read from the bottom upwards
the second part of the wordplay is placed after the first, setting the order of the pieces

blocks.note: lid is slang for a hat
the Roman numeral for one
a gent is a man; the 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition

explanation.surface: A bachelor who doffs his hat is being polite and attentive to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of man's is read as 'is', the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone diligent is careful and painstaking, paying close heed to a task, so it is a near synonym.

clue.text: Plant is further up the wall

blocks.note: first meaning: a plant whose root gives a red dye
second meaning: more crazy, as 'up the wall' means mad

explanation.surface: A climbing plant has reached higher up a garden wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up the wall' looks like a gardening location but is the idiom for being driven mad, so 'further' asks for the comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: Madder is both the dye plant Rubia and the comparative of mad, matching the idiom 'up the wall'.

clue.text: Film copper in case of sadism

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so only its outer letters are kept
one element is placed inside another, which encloses it

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A movie about a police officer investigating a sadism case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' and 'copper' suggest a cop movie, but film here is a surface layer of grime.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is a layer of dirt or froth on a liquid, a sense of film as a thin coating.

indicators.note: things that are shifting move about, so these letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A driver changing up to a higher gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Higher gear' reads as one motoring phrase; 'Higher' alone is the definition, in its sense of meat that has gone off.
explanation.definitionFit: Game hung until strong-smelling is called high, so meat that is higher is gamier, more strongly flavoured.

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so one word wraps round another

blocks.note: impious means lacking reverence
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword Queen

explanation.surface: A haughty, disrespectful courtier hugging the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperious describes a domineering, haughty manner, so it is a synonym of overbearing and arrogant.

clue.text: Bad end in Iran once changing rule

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is all that is kept
letters that are changing are rearranged into a different order

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim conclusion in Iran when a former rule changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad end' looks like a grim outcome but only asks for a final letter; 'in' simply places it with the other fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative decree or regulation, which is a rule laid down by authority.

blocks.note: to bar is to stop or block
the setter, or compiler, refers to their own as my

explanation.surface: Someone shouts that the crossword setter has gone off for lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out to lunch' pretends to be a literal absence; it is the idiom for crazy. Barmy is British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'out to lunch' means mentally absent or crazy, matching the slang adjective for daft.

indicators.note: a word's leader is the letter at its front, so only the first letter is used
one piece goes after the other, fixing which comes first

blocks.note: drive is motive power, as in a car's drive
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Dismissing a Labour Party leader who has come after someone in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' tempts a name such as Foot or Blair; it only wants the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivel is silly nonsense, so it is a synonym of rubbish in the sense of worthless talk.

clue.text: Rotten gripped by punk in Damned

indicators.note: what is gripped is held inside, so the letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across these three words

explanation.surface: Johnny Rotten held by a punk from the band the Damned.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotten looks like Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols, and the Damned were a punk band; the clue's capital R just starts the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Being rotten to someone means treating them nastily, so the adjective is an informal synonym for cruel.

clue.text: Disciplinarian demands neat trim turn out

indicators.note: to turn something out is to tip it up and rearrange it, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A strict sergeant insists that recruits look neat and trim on parade.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a strict enforcer of rules, named after a French drillmaster, so the word means a stern disciplinarian.

indicators.note: one that is chasing runs behind, so this part follows the other

blocks.note: a teacher's pet is a favourite
re means about or concerning
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A favourite bird chasing around a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The petrel is a seabird of the open ocean, so it is a particular example of a bird.

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: a rave is a wild party, a revel

explanation.surface: A pub that lets clubbers hold a rave.
explanation.walkthrough: Bar looks like a pub, but it is a metal rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A lever is a rigid rod used to prise or lift, so it is a kind of bar such as a crowbar.

indicators.note: what is reported is spoken, so the word is judged by how it sounds when said

blocks.note: verging, as in verging on, means touching or bordering, said with the final g dropped

explanation.surface: A paradox: something both untouched and touching at once.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone needs verging said casually as 'vergin'; verging on something is touching its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgin snow or territory is pristine and never handled or explored, so the adjective means unspoilt.

indicators.note: one word goes inside the other, which surrounds it

blocks.note: a rest is a support, as for a snooker cue
an express is a fast train

explanation.surface: Speaking up in favour of moderate policies.
explanation.walkthrough: Express looks like a verb, to voice; it is the noun for a fast train.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is holding oneself back from excess, so it is a synonym of self-control and temperance.

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school exercise
ST is the abbreviation for street; on places it after the first piece

explanation.surface: Working out on the road leaves you sore.
explanation.walkthrough: Pain looks physical after exercise, but here it means a nuisance, as in 'a pain'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pest is an annoying person or thing, and 'a pain' is the informal idiom for exactly that.

clue.text: In front of line, threw hammer

indicators.note: being in front means coming earlier, so this part precedes the other

blocks.note: threw a party or a punch, gave one
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: An athlete stepping to the line and throwing the hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: The hammer of the athletics surface is the small mallet a judge or auctioneer bangs.
explanation.definitionFit: A gavel is the small wooden mallet an auctioneer or chairman strikes, so it is a kind of hammer.

blocks.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
the Forest of Arden, setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: An estate whose grounds include a magnificent forest.
explanation.definitionFit: The grounds of a house are the land around it, and a garden is that cultivated plot, a near synonym.

blocks.note: first meaning: the French word meaning for
second meaning: to tip a liquid out of a jug

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look as if the clue wants the French for tip, pourboire; instead 'French for' is one meaning and tip the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The French preposition for 'for' is also the English verb for tipping liquid from a container.

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly
able means competent

explanation.surface: A genuine friend who gets on with the job without fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Palpable means able to be touched or felt, so something palpable is tangible and real.

indicators.note: a translation turns words into a different form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Reading Proust in translation sends you to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the reputation of Proust's very long novel for putting readers to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a state of near unconsciousness, close in sense to a coma.

clue.text: Seen in Capri, so not cooler!

indicators.note: what is seen in something is visible within it, here inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across these three words

explanation.surface: A tourist complaining that Capri was not as cool as hoped.
explanation.walkthrough: Cooler looks like a comparative about the weather; it is slang for a jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooler is old slang for a jail cell, so it names a place of confinement.

indicators.note: placed by something means set beside it, so the two parts join end to end

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for river
to amble is to walk slowly

explanation.surface: Encouraging someone to take a riverside walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on' reads as encouragement, but it is the definition: to talk on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: To ramble is to talk at length without focus, which is what going on means in speech.

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, its first letter, which alone is kept
to catch something is to hold it, so one word goes around another

blocks.note: Édouard Manet, the French painter
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: One painter sketching a portrait of another, Goya.
explanation.walkthrough: Draw sits beside artist as if it meant sketch; it means attraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet is something that attracts, and a draw is an attraction that pulls people in.

indicators.note: what is following comes after, so this part goes second

blocks.note: w is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a wide, a ball bowled out of reach
an edge is a boundary

explanation.surface: A cricket shot sliced to the boundary off a wide delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: Slice, boundary and wide all suggest cricket; slice is the definition as a noun, a wedge-shaped piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedge of cheese or cake is a triangular portion, so it is a slice.

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the printed compound splits in two: its front half is the definition and its back half starts the fodder
taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A performance is about to start and the audience is thrilled.
explanation.walkthrough: Showtime looks like one word; it splits into the definition Show and the first word of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To manifest something is to display or reveal it plainly, so the verb is a synonym of show.

blocks.note: first meaning: the laurel or bay is an example of this plant
second meaning: Herbert Beerbohm ..., the Victorian actor-manager

explanation.walkthrough: Laurel suggests Stan Laurel, so the solver hunts a comedian; the answer is a plant, and the actor is Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree, who founded RADA.
explanation.definitionFit: The laurel is an evergreen woody plant, an example of the category, and Tree was a famous London stage actor.

blocks.note: first meaning: a wine from the Bordeaux region
second meaning: burial chambers

explanation.walkthrough: Wine vaults suggests cellars; the two words are separate meanings. Graves is a Bordeaux wine district.
explanation.definitionFit: Graves names a Bordeaux wine, and burial places such as tombs are vaults, so the plural noun matches both.

clue.text: Includes nickel, gold or tin initially

definitions.text: Includes nickel, gold or tin initially

indicators.note: initially points to the start of each word, so only first letters are used

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A description of metal bars made of nickel, gold or tin.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: the first letters spell the answer, and the sentence describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingot is a cast block of metal, which could be nickel, gold or tin, so the clue describes one.

blocks.note: surface reading: botany or forestry, the science of woods
setter's reading: family trees, the charts of descent from ancestors

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the trees are not plants but family trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Genealogy is the research of ancestry and lines of descent, which are drawn up as family trees.
